Seminar Title:

Development and Characterization of Zein- and Soy Protein Isolate-Derived Amyloid Hydrogels for Wound Healing Applications

Abstract:

Wound healing is a complex and highly coordinated biological process involving inflammation, cell proliferation, tissue regeneration, angiogenesis, and extracellular matrix remodelling. However, chronic wounds often exhibit impaired healing due to persistent inflammation, oxidative stress, microbial infection, and inadequate tissue regeneration. Conventional wound dressings often fail to address these multifactorial challenges. Therefore, hydrogels have emerged as promising wound dressings due to their high water-retention capacity, biocompatibility, tunable mechanical properties, and ability to maintain a moist environment. Additionally, amyloid-based hydrogels can be synthesized to achieve desirable structural and functional characteristics. Although, amyloids are historically associated with pathological protein aggregation, functional amyloids have gained recognition as versatile biomolecular building blocks for biomedical applications. Amyloids are highly ordered protein aggregates characterised by cross &beta-sheet architecture, formed through the self-assembly of peptides or proteins under specific physicochemical conditions. Their hierarchical assembly, structural stability, and high surface area provide opportunities for hydrogel development.&nbsp Therefore, this study aims to synthesize amyloid-based hydrogels from Soy protein Isolate (SPI) and Zein protein for wound healing applications. The presence of &beta - sheets was analyzed by the Thioflavin T (ThT) assay and 8-Anilinonaphthalene-1-sulfonic acid (ANS) assay. Further characterization of &beta - sheets was done by Circular Dichroism (CD) and Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy. The SPI fibrils were confirmed by Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscopy (FESEM).
